Scafell Pike.about: England's highest mountain: a bouldery dome topped by a huge summit cairn, a trig point and the war memorial plaque given with the summit to the National Trust.

routes.name: Wasdale Head via Brown Tongue
routes.text: The shortest way. Up Lingmell Gill and the steep pitched path of Brown Tongue into Hollow Stones, then left up the bouldery slope to the top.

routes.name: Seathwaite via the Corridor Route
routes.text: From Borrowdale by Stockley Bridge to Sty Head, then the Corridor Route across the flank of Great End and Lingmell to the summit plateau.

routes.name: Great Langdale via Esk Hause
routes.text: Up Mickleden and Rossett Gill to Angle Tarn and Esk Hause, then the rough boulder ridge over Ill Crag and Broad Crag.

Scafell.photo: Sca Fell Summit Cairn and Symonds Knott. - geograph.org.uk - 246540.jpg
Scafell.about: Scafell Pike's rockier, quieter neighbour across the gap of Mickledore. Broad Stand, the direct way between them, is a serious rock climb, not a walk.

routes.name: Wasdale Head via Green How
routes.text: A relentless grassy slope from Brackenclose straight up the west side; the easiest way up, if steep.

routes.name: From Scafell Pike via Foxes Tarn
routes.text: Drop from Mickledore on the Eskdale side, then climb the gully past tiny Foxes Tarn. The usual way to add Scafell to the Pike.

routes.name: Eskdale via Slight Side
routes.text: From Boot across the moor past Eel Tarn to Slight Side, then up the long south ridge. Long and quiet.

Helvellyn.about: The Lakes' most popular big fell: a broad summit plateau above the Red Tarn corrie, held between the arms of Striding Edge and Swirral Edge.

routes.name: Glenridding via Striding Edge
routes.text: The classic scramble. Up to the Hole-in-the-Wall, along the exposed rocky crest of Striding Edge, then a steep loose wall to the plateau.

routes.name: Glenridding via Swirral Edge
routes.text: Past Red Tarn and up the shorter, easier ridge beside Catstye Cam; the usual way down after Striding Edge.

routes.name: Thirlmere from Swirls
routes.text: The quickest way: a steep pitched path over Browncove Crags from the Swirls car park on the A591.

routes.name: Bridleway along the ridge
routes.text: The main ridge path from Grisedale Tarn over Dollywaggon and Nethermost Pike to the summit, and north towards Whiteside, is a public bridleway: a hard, rocky but legal ride.

Skiddaw.about: A great slaty whaleback above Keswick, with a long, stony summit ridge and a trig point; one of the few big Lakeland summits on a bridleway.

routes.name: Keswick via Jenkin Hill
routes.text: From the car park above Latrigg, the broad 'tourist' path climbs Jenkin Hill and skirts Little Man. Long and steady, and a bridleway all the way to the summit.

routes.name: Millbeck via Carl Side
routes.text: Steep and direct from Millbeck up Carl Side, then loose scree to the summit ridge.

routes.name: Back o' Skiddaw via Bakestall
routes.text: From the road end near Peter House Farm, the track past Whitewater Dash waterfall, then the steep Bakestall ridge from the north.

Great End.about: The dark, gully-scored northern end of the Scafell massif, looming over Sprinkling Tarn and Borrowdale. Its gullies are classic winter climbs.

routes.name: Seathwaite via Grains Gill
routes.text: Up Grains Gill and Ruddy Gill to Esk Hause, then turn north-west up the broad slope to the summit cairns.

routes.name: Great Langdale via Rossett Gill
routes.text: Over Rossett Pass and past Angle Tarn to Esk Hause, then up the stony slope.

routes.name: With Scafell Pike
routes.text: Often added on the way to or from the Pike: about 1.5 km of boulders over Ill Crag and Broad Crag.

Bowfell.about: A shapely rock peak at the head of Great Langdale. The Great Slab and the Climbers' Traverse on its north-east face are among the Lakes' best walking terrain.

routes.name: Great Langdale via The Band
routes.text: From the Old Dungeon Ghyll, up the long ridge of The Band to Three Tarns, then north over the boulder-strewn final cone.

routes.name: The Climbers' Traverse
routes.text: From the top of The Band, a narrow path under Flat Crags to the Great Slab and a steep, rocky finish. More interesting, a little more exposed.

routes.name: Eskdale via Lingcove Beck
routes.text: A long, quiet approach from Brotherilkeld up Lingcove Beck to Three Tarns.

Great Gable.about: The rock pyramid between Wasdale and Borrowdale. A bronze war memorial on the summit crag draws a crowd every Remembrance Sunday.

routes.name: Honister via Green Gable
routes.text: From the slate mine, up the old tramway to the Drum House, then over Brandreth and Green Gable to Windy Gap and a steep rocky finish. Starts high.

routes.name: Wasdale Head via Sty Head
routes.text: Up the valley to Sty Head, then the steep, rocky south-east ridge.

routes.name: Seathwaite via Sty Head
routes.text: Stockley Bridge and Styhead Gill to Sty Head, then the same rough ridge.

Pillar.photo: Trig point and cairn on summit of Pillar - geograph.org.uk - 7625011.jpg
Pillar.about: The highest fell between Wasdale and Ennerdale, named after Pillar Rock, the great crag on its northern face, first climbed in 1826.

routes.name: Wasdale Head via Black Sail Pass
routes.text: Up Mosedale to Black Sail Pass, then west along the ridge over Looking Stead.

routes.name: The High Level Route
routes.text: From Looking Stead, a narrow, exposed path traverses under the north face to Robinson's Cairn and Pillar Rock, then climbs steeply to the top.

routes.name: Ennerdale
routes.text: From Bowness Knott, the long Ennerdale forest road (good on a bike) to the head of the valley, then up from Black Sail Hut. A big day.

Nethermost Pike.about: A flat-topped summit on the Helvellyn ridge just south of the main top, with a steep craggy face above Grisedale. Many people pass by without noticing it.

routes.name: Along the ridge from Helvellyn
routes.text: Under a kilometre south along the broad ridge; the main path skirts the top, so step west to find the cairn.

routes.name: Wythburn
routes.text: From Wythburn church on Thirlmere, up the pitched path to the ridge, then north.

routes.name: Grisedale via the east ridge
routes.text: From Patterdale along Grisedale, then up the steep, rough and quiet east ridge.

routes.name: Bridleway along the ridge
routes.text: The ridge path from Grisedale Tarn to Helvellyn, beside the summit, is a public bridleway.

Catstye Cam.about: A perfect little cone at the end of Swirral Edge, and the best perch above Red Tarn.

routes.name: Glenridding via Red Tarn Beck
routes.text: Past the old Greenside lead mine and up Red Tarn Beck, then the steep path onto the north-east ridge.

routes.name: From Swirral Edge
routes.text: A short there-and-back from the foot of Swirral Edge on the way up or down Helvellyn.

Urra Moor.photo: Round Hill trig point, Urra Moor - geograph.org.uk - 7548796.jpg
Urra Moor.about: Round Hill on Urra Moor is the highest point of the North York Moors: a trig point on a Bronze Age burial mound, beside the carved Hand Stone guide post.

routes.name: Clay Bank via the Cleveland Way
routes.text: From the Clay Bank car park on the B1257, up the steep climb of Carr Ridge, then east along the broad moorland track.

routes.name: Ingleby Incline
routes.text: From Ingleby Greenhow, up the old Ingleby Incline (a bridleway, the ironstone railway's rope-hauled incline) to Bloworth Crossing, then west along the Cleveland Way. A well-known mountain bike climb.

Cringle Moor.photo: Cleveland plain and Roseberry Topping from Cringle Moor - geograph.org.uk - 1429492.jpg
Cringle Moor.about: A steep-sided moor on the northern escarpment of the Cleveland Hills. The summit is the Drake Howe burial mound; a stone seat and view indicator on Cringle End look out over the Cleveland plain.

routes.name: Lord Stones
routes.text: From the Lord Stones café car park, the Cleveland Way climbs east to the viewpoint on Cringle End; the summit is a short way along the edge.

routes.name: The Three Sisters from Clay Bank
routes.text: West along the Cleveland Way over Hasty Bank and Cold Moor, a switchback of steep drops and climbs along the escarpment.

Stony Ridge.photo: Large boundary stone on Stony Ridge - geograph.org.uk - 7413897.jpg
Stony Ridge.about: A barely-noticeable heather rise on the high watershed above the head of Farndale, scattered with old boundary stones.

routes.name: Old Rosedale railway
routes.text: The trackbed of the old ironstone railway round the head of Farndale, a bridleway and part of the Lyke Wake Walk, passes about a kilometre away; a moor track runs closer.

routes.name: From Blakey Ridge
routes.text: From the Lion Inn at Blakey, follow the railway trackbed west round the head of Farndale. Easy, level going.

Cockayne Ridge.about: The moor at the head of Bransdale, above the hamlet of Cockayne; a broad heather plateau rather than a ridge.

routes.name: Rudland Rigg
routes.text: The old road along Rudland Rigg, between Bransdale and Farndale, passes about a kilometre east. A famous long moorland track for riders, from Gillamoor north to Bloworth Crossing.

routes.name: From the head of Bransdale
routes.text: From the road end near Cockayne, up the moor on shooting tracks.

Ledging Hill.photo: Old Wayside Cross on Ledging Hill, Blakey Ridge, Westerdale Parish (geograph 6044799).jpg
Ledging Hill.about: A summit at Rosedale Head, crowned by Old Ralph, one of the medieval stone crosses beside the moor road. Its neighbour Young Ralph is the emblem of the National Park.

routes.name: Blakey Ridge road
routes.text: The moor road from Hutton-le-Hole and the Lion Inn to Castleton passes within 300 m; walk across to Old Ralph from Ralph Cross at the road junction.

routes.name: Old Rosedale railway
routes.text: The trackbed of the ironstone railway from Blakey runs round Rosedale Head about a kilometre to the south.

Carlton Bank.photo: Trig point and boundary stone on Carlton Bank - geograph.org.uk - 4495634.jpg
Carlton Bank.about: The western end of the Cleveland Hills escarpment above Carlton-in-Cleveland, with a trig point, a gliding club and a huge view over the Tees plain.

routes.name: Lord Stones
routes.text: From the Lord Stones café car park, a short, steep climb west on the Cleveland Way.

routes.name: Carlton-in-Cleveland
routes.text: Up the steep lane to the top of Carlton Bank, then the Cleveland Way to the trig.

Noon Hill.about: A heather top on Bilsdale West Moor near the Green Howe burial mounds, north of the Bilsdale TV mast.

routes.name: From Chop Gate
routes.text: From Chop Gate in Bilsdale, climb west onto Bilsdale West Moor by the bridleway past Cock Howe, then north along the moor.

routes.name: From Raisdale
routes.text: From the Raisdale road, up the moor tracks from the north.

Cock Heads.about: A broad, featureless heather top on the moor between the heads of Rosedale and Glaisdale.

routes.name: From Rosedale Head
routes.text: From the Knott Road or the Blakey road at Rosedale Head, east across the moor on paths and shooting tracks.

routes.name: George Gap and Cut Road
routes.text: Two moorland bridleways, George Gap and Cut Road, cross the moor about a kilometre from the top.

Cock Howe.about: A Bronze Age burial mound on Bilsdale West Moor, with an old boundary stone beside it.

routes.name: From Chop Gate
routes.text: From Chop Gate in Bilsdale, the bridleway west over Bilsdale West Moor towards Hawnby passes right by the mound.

routes.name: Along the moor from Noon Hill
routes.text: Half a kilometre south of Noon Hill on the moor path.

Black Hambleton.about: The northern end of the Hambleton Hills, crossed by the Hambleton Drove Road, an ancient cattle droving route now followed by the Cleveland Way.

routes.name: Square Corner via the Drove Road
routes.text: From Square Corner above Osmotherley, south along the Cleveland Way on the old Hambleton Street, a byway popular with riders, then a short climb to the trig.

routes.name: From Kepwick or Over Silton
routes.text: Steep bridleways climb the western escarpment from the villages below to join the Drove Road.

Whernside.about: The highest of the Yorkshire Three Peaks and of the Dales: a long ridge above the Ribblehead Viaduct on the Settle–Carlisle line.

routes.name: Ribblehead
routes.text: Past the viaduct and up beside the railway, then by Force Gill onto the ridge and south along it. The Three Peaks route.

routes.name: Chapel-le-Dale
routes.text: Steep and direct up the stone steps from Bruntscar.

routes.name: Dentdale
routes.text: From Dentdale, the Craven Way, an old packhorse track, climbs over the north-east shoulder; leave it for the ridge.

Ingleborough.about: A flat-topped gritstone fortress, ringed by the remains of an Iron Age hillfort wall, with a cross-shaped wind shelter and a trig point.

routes.name: Clapham via Gaping Gill
routes.text: Past Ingleborough Cave and through the limestone gorge of Trow Gill to the Gaping Gill pothole, then up Little Ingleborough.

routes.name: Ingleton via Crina Bottom
routes.text: Up Fell Lane and past Crina Bottom farm to the steep final climb. Fell Lane is a bridleway all the way to the summit.

routes.name: Chapel-le-Dale
routes.text: The Three Peaks route across Humphrey Bottom and up the stone staircase.

Great Shunner Fell.about: The third-highest fell in the Dales, a broad grassy hill between Wensleydale and Swaledale crossed by the Pennine Way.

routes.name: Hardraw on the Pennine Way
routes.text: From Hardraw near Hawes, the Pennine Way climbs the long, gentle south-east ridge. Easy to follow, flagged across the boggy parts.

routes.name: Thwaite on the Pennine Way
routes.text: From Thwaite in Swaledale, steadily up the north-east ridge.

High Seat.about: The highest point of Mallerstang Edge, the long gritstone escarpment above the head of the Eden valley.

routes.name: From Mallerstang
routes.text: The usual way, from the valley road (B6259) at Outhgill, steeply up the western flank onto the edge.

routes.name: Along Mallerstang Edge
routes.text: North from Hugh Seat and Lady Anne's Pillar, or south from the Kirkby Stephen–Keld road, along the rough, wet top of the edge.

Wild Boar Fell.about: A flat-topped fell with a dramatic gritstone scarp above Mallerstang, where the last wild boar in England was said to have been killed.

routes.name: From Mallerstang via The Nab
routes.text: From the B6259, under the Settle–Carlisle railway and up to The Nab, the fell's northern prow, then along the edge.

routes.name: Ridge from Swarth Fell
routes.text: Along the grassy ridge from Swarth Fell to the south, often walked as a horseshoe from Aisgill.

Great Whernside.about: A long gritstone ridge between Wharfedale and Nidderdale with a rocky summit crest; not to be confused with Whernside.

routes.name: Kettlewell via Hag Dyke
routes.text: Up past Hag Dyke, an old farmhouse that is now a scout hostel, and the steep edge to the summit rocks.

routes.name: Park Rash
routes.text: From the top of the steep Kettlewell–Coverdale road, south along the ridge.

Buckden Pike.about: A broad top above Upper Wharfedale with a memorial cross to five Polish airmen killed when their Wellington bomber crashed here in a blizzard in 1942.

routes.name: Buckden
routes.text: From the village car park, a path climbs steadily up the hillside to the summit ridge and the trig point by the wall.

routes.name: Starbotton
routes.text: Up the Walden Road bridleway from Starbotton to the ridge, then north past the memorial cross.

Pen-y-ghent.about: A lion-shaped hill above Horton in Ribblesdale, the smallest and most distinctive of the Three Peaks.

routes.name: Horton via Brackenbottom
routes.text: Up past Brackenbottom farm to the stepped nose of the hill and a short scramble up its rocky tiers.

routes.name: Horton via Hunt Pot
routes.text: The Pennine Way up Horton Scar Lane (a bridleway), then past the potholes of Hull Pot and Hunt Pot.

Great Coum.about: A quiet top above Dentdale. The County Stone just below it once marked where Yorkshire, Lancashire and Westmorland met.

routes.name: Dent via Flinter Gill
routes.text: Up the steep, stony lane of Flinter Gill to the Occupation Road (a bridleway well known to riders), then up beside the wall.

routes.name: White Shaw Moss
routes.text: The shortest way, from the minor road between Dent and Kingsdale.

Great Coum.author: T Eyre

Swarth Fell.about: A quiet fell on the ridge south of Wild Boar Fell, above the Settle–Carlisle railway's summit at Aisgill.

routes.name: Horseshoe from Aisgill
routes.text: From the B6259 near Aisgill, up onto the ridge and over both Swarth Fell and Wild Boar Fell.

routes.name: Ridge from Wild Boar Fell
routes.text: South along the grassy ridge past a line of tarns.

Cross Fell.about: The highest point of the Pennines and of England outside the Lake District: a stony plateau with a cross-shaped shelter, home of the Helm Wind.

routes.name: Pennine Way from Dufton
routes.text: The classic high day: over Knock Fell, Great Dun Fell and Little Dun Fell. Long, exposed, but well marked.

routes.name: Kirkland
routes.text: Up the old corpse road bridleway towards Greg's Hut, then leave it for the path up the western escarpment.

routes.name: Garrigill via Greg's Hut
routes.text: The long, gentle corpse road from Garrigill (a well-known ride over to Kirkland) climbs to Greg's Hut bothy; then the Pennine Way to the top.

Great Dun Fell.about: Crowned by the white radar dome of an air traffic control station, reached by the highest paved road in Britain: private, closed to cars, open to walkers and cyclists.

routes.name: The radar road from Knock
routes.text: A famously hard road climb on tarmac all the way to the gate below the radar station.

routes.name: Pennine Way from Dufton
routes.text: Over Knock Fell and across the slabs to the summit.

Little Dun Fell.photo: Great Dun Fell from Little Dun Fell - geograph.org.uk - 6106745.jpg
Little Dun Fell.about: A small top with a stone shelter between Great Dun Fell and Cross Fell, on the Pennine Way.

routes.name: From Great Dun Fell
routes.text: North along the stone-slabbed Pennine Way from the end of the radar road.

routes.name: Pennine Way from Dufton
routes.text: Over Knock Fell and Great Dun Fell; usually walked on the way to Cross Fell.

Knock Fell.about: The first big top on the Pennine Way north of Dufton, with the large cairn of Knock Old Man; part of the Moor House–Upper Teesdale nature reserve.

routes.name: Pennine Way from Dufton
routes.text: Steeply up beside Swindale Beck to the big Knock Old Man cairn and the summit plateau.

routes.name: From Great Dun Fell
routes.text: South along the Pennine Way from the radar road.

Mickle Fell.about: Once the highest point in Yorkshire, now in County Durham: a long whaleback in remote, boggy moor inside the Warcop army training area.

routes.name: Access is restricted
routes.text: The fell is in a live firing range. Go only when the range is open to the public and keep to the permitted access routes; check the Ministry of Defence's Warcop access times first.

routes.name: From Teesdale or the Eden Valley
routes.text: Long hikes over rough moor from either side; a track runs along the summit ridge.

Meldon Hill.about: A broad, remote moor in the Moor House–Upper Teesdale nature reserve, between Cow Green Reservoir and the head of High Cup Nick. The trig point has been wrecked.

routes.name: From the Pennine Way
routes.text: A track crosses the summit. Most people come over rough moor from the Pennine Way where it passes between Cauldron Snout and High Cup Nick.

Little Fell.about: Mickle Fell's southern neighbour above the Eden Valley, its trig point broken; also inside the Warcop army training area.

routes.name: Access is restricted
routes.text: Like Mickle Fell it is in a live firing range: go only when the range is open to the public, and check the Ministry of Defence's Warcop access times first.

routes.name: From Hilton
routes.text: From Hilton in the Eden Valley, a track climbs beside Hilton Beck towards the old mines, then the steep western slopes. Only when the range is open.

Burnhope Seat.photo: Trig point on Burnhope Seat - geograph.org.uk - 1444972.jpg
Burnhope Seat.about: A wide, boggy plateau of peat and tussock grass on the Durham–Cumbria border, with the Yad Moss ski tows on its north-west slope.

routes.name: Yad Moss
routes.text: The easiest way: from the B6277 Alston–Middleton road at Yad Moss, about 2 km of rough, wet moor to the trig.

routes.name: Burnhope Reservoir circuit
routes.text: From Wearhead, a high-level round of the moors above Burnhope Reservoir.

Melmerby Fell.about: A high point of the western Pennine escarpment above the Eden Valley, with a cairn and a currick (a Pennine cairn) on Dun Edge.

routes.name: The Maiden Way
routes.text: The Roman road over the fells from Kirkland towards Alston is a bridleway passing about half a kilometre east of the top. A stiff ride.

routes.name: From Hartside
routes.text: South from the Hartside pass on the A686 along the edge of the escarpment.

Great Stony Hill.photo: Summit knoll and trig on Great Stony Hill - geograph.org.uk - 7957799.jpg
Great Stony Hill.about: A moorland top between Weardale and Teesdale, its trig point on a small knoll among old lead mine workings.

routes.name: From the B6277
routes.text: The Alston–Middleton road passes about 1.3 km west of the top; a moorland track passes within 350 m of it.

Ben Macdui.about: Britain's second-highest mountain: a vast stony plateau with a view indicator, said to be haunted by the Big Grey Man, Am Fear Liath Mòr.

routes.name: From the Cairn Gorm ski centre
routes.text: From the Coire Cas car park, up the ridge of Fiacaill a' Choire Chais, then across the plateau past Lochan Buidhe. Navigation is serious in mist.

routes.name: Linn of Dee via Derry Lodge
routes.text: Ride the estate track to Derry Lodge, then walk up Glen Luibeg and the long Sròn Riach ridge or by Loch Etchachan.

Braeriach.about: Britain's third-highest summit, perched on the rim of huge corries above the Lairig Ghru. The River Dee rises at the Wells of Dee on its plateau.

routes.name: Chalamain Gap
routes.text: From the Sugar Bowl car park on the ski road, through the bouldery Chalamain Gap, down into the Lairig Ghru and up the Sròn na Lairige ridge.

routes.name: Gleann Einich
routes.text: Ride the long Gleann Einich track from Whitewell or Coylumbridge, then up Coire Dhondail onto the plateau and round the corrie rim.

Cairn Toul.about: A pointed summit on the west rim of the Lairig Ghru, Britain's fourth-highest, usually climbed with Braeriach and the Angel's Peak.

routes.name: From Braeriach
routes.text: Round the rim of the plateau and over the Angel's Peak: the classic high Cairngorm traverse.

routes.name: Corrour Bothy
routes.text: From Linn of Dee via Derry Lodge and the Lairig Ghru to Corrour Bothy, then up the Coire Odhar path to the ridge.

Sgor an Lochain Uaine.about: The Angel's Peak: a sharp top above the green lochan of Garbh Choire, between Braeriach and Cairn Toul.

routes.name: Braeriach to Cairn Toul
routes.text: Climbed on the traverse between them, from Braeriach round the corrie rim or a short climb from the col with Cairn Toul.

Cairn Gorm.about: The mountain that names the range, above the ski area, with a weather station on top and the Ptarmigan station of the funicular railway just below.

routes.name: Windy Ridge
routes.text: From the Coire Cas car park up the Sròn an Aonaich ridge beside the ski tows, past the Ptarmigan station to the summit.

routes.name: Northern corries
routes.text: Up Fiacaill a' Choire Chais and round the cliff tops of Coire an t-Sneachda, a fine high circuit.

Beinn a' Bhùird.about: A huge flat-topped mountain in the eastern Cairngorms, ringed by fine corries; the North Top is its highest point.

routes.name: Glen Quoich and An Diollaid
routes.text: From the car park at Allanaquoich, up Glen Quoich, then the path on the line of the old Land Rover road up An Diollaid to the plateau and north to the top. Often biked to the start of the climb.

routes.name: Quoich Water to The Sneck
routes.text: Through the pinewoods along the Quoich Water to The Sneck, the col with Ben Avon.

Beinn Mheadhoin.about: The 'middle hill': a remote plateau studded with granite tors between Loch Avon and Loch Etchachan.

routes.name: From the Cairn Gorm ski centre
routes.text: Across the plateau and down to the head of Loch Avon by the Shelter Stone, then up past Loch Etchachan.

routes.name: Linn of Dee via Glen Derry
routes.text: Ride to Derry Lodge, walk up Glen Derry to Loch Etchachan, then up the broad south-west slope.

Ben Avon.about: A sprawling plateau dotted with granite tors. The top, Leabaidh an Daimh Bhuidhe, is a tor you must scramble up to touch the highest point.

routes.name: Via The Sneck
routes.text: Up the glen between Ben Avon and Beinn a' Bhùird to The Sneck, the col between them; often combined with Beinn a' Bhùird.

routes.name: Gleann an t-Slugain
routes.text: From Keiloch near Braemar, the track through Gleann an t-Slugain (good on a bike), then the long southern slopes, passing close to the rim of the Slochd Mòr corrie.

routes.name: Glen Avon
routes.text: From Tomintoul along the long Glen Avon track; one of the remotest approaches in the Cairngorms.

Beinn Bhrotain.about: A broad, bouldery dome at the south end of the Cairn Toul ridge, above Glen Dee and Glen Geusachan.

routes.name: Linn of Dee via White Bridge
routes.text: Ride the track to the White Bridge and up Glen Dee, then climb the south-east slopes. Often combined with Monadh Mòr.

Lochnagar.photo: Lochnagar - Mountain and Corrie Lochan. - geograph.org.uk - 113301.jpg
Lochnagar.about: The royal mountain above Balmoral: a great cliff-ringed corrie and loch beneath a summit ridge whose top is Cac Càrn Beag.

routes.name: Spittal of Glenmuick
routes.text: Up the track to the col below Meikle Pap, then the steep 'Ladder' path and round the rim of the corrie.

routes.name: Circuit via the Glas Allt
routes.text: Return down past the Glas Allt falls to Loch Muick for a fine round.

Ben More.about: The highest mountain in the National Park, a huge steep cone above Crianlarich.

routes.name: Benmore Farm
routes.text: From Benmore Farm on the A85, a relentless climb up the north-west shoulder: almost all ascent and no respite.

routes.name: With Stob Binnein
routes.text: Down to the Bealach-eadar-dhà Bheinn and up Stob Binnein, returning down Benmore Glen.

Stob Binnein.about: Ben More's twin, with a distinctive cone that looks sliced off at the top.

routes.name: Inverlochlarig
routes.text: From the road end in Balquhidder Glen, up the south ridge over Stob Coire an Lochain.

routes.name: From Ben More
routes.text: Down to the bealach between them and up the steep north ridge.

Ben Lui.about: One of the finest Munros: a great north-east corrie, Coire Gaothach, often holding snow into spring.

routes.name: Glen Cononish
routes.text: From Dalrigh near Tyndrum, the track up Glen Cononish past the gold mine (rideable to the end), then into Coire Gaothach and up its north-east ridge.

routes.name: Glen Lochy
routes.text: Shorter but wetter: from the A85, cross the river and the railway, then up the forest and Fionn Choirein.

Cruach Ardrain.photo: Cruach Ardrain from Beinn Tulaichean - geograph.org.uk - 87786.jpg
Cruach Ardrain.about: A complex hill of ridges and corries south of Crianlarich, with Beinn Tulaichean as its southern top.

routes.name: Crianlarich
routes.text: From the A82, through the forest and up the Grey Height ridge over Meall Dhamh.

routes.name: Inverlochlarig via Beinn Tulaichean
routes.text: From Balquhidder Glen, up the grassy south ridge over Beinn Tulaichean.

Ben Oss.photo: Ben Oss and Beinn Dubhcraig (Explored 24-04-24) - Flickr - jkiscycling.jpg
Ben Oss.about: A shapely peak between Ben Lui and Beinn Dubhchraig, above Loch Oss.

routes.name: Dalrigh with Beinn Dubhchraig
routes.text: From Dalrigh, through the Caledonian pinewood of Coille Coire Chuilc and up Beinn Dubhchraig, then over the bealach to Ben Oss.

Beinn Ìme.about: The highest of the Arrochar Alps, a bulky hill above the Rest and Be Thankful.

routes.name: Succoth via Bealach a' Mhàim
routes.text: From the head of Loch Long, the Cobbler path into the corrie, then over Bealach a' Mhàim and up the south-east slopes.

routes.name: Butterbridge
routes.text: Short and steep from Glen Kinglas on the A83.

An Caisteal.photo: An Caisteal summit from Twistin Hill.jpg
An Caisteal.about: 'The castle': a rocky summit at the head of Glen Falloch, reached by the long north ridge of Twistin Hill.

routes.name: Glen Falloch via Twistin Hill
routes.text: From the A82 south of Crianlarich, under the railway, up Sròn Gharbh and along Twistin Hill. Often climbed with Beinn a' Chroin.

Ben Vorlich.about: A neat pointed summit with a trig point above Loch Earn, and one of the great viewpoints of the southern Highlands.

routes.name: Ardvorlich
routes.text: From Ardvorlich on the south shore of Loch Earn, up Glen Vorlich on a track, then the clear north ridge path.

routes.name: With Stùc a' Chroin
routes.text: Down the south-west ridge to the Bealach an Dubh Choirein and up Stùc a' Chroin.

Beinn Dubhchraig.photo: Bealach between Ben Oss and Ben Dubhchraig - geograph.org.uk - 122147.jpg
Beinn Dubhchraig.about: A broad hill rising above the Caledonian pinewood of Coille Coire Chuilc, west of Tyndrum.

routes.name: Dalrigh
routes.text: Through the pinewood and up beside the Allt Coire Dubhchraig to the north-east ridge. Usually combined with Ben Oss.

Stùc a' Chroin.about: Ben Vorlich's craggy neighbour, guarded on the north by a steep buttress.

routes.name: Over Ben Vorlich
routes.text: From Ardvorlich over Ben Vorlich to the Bealach an Dubh Choirein, then steep rough paths with scrambling up the right side of the buttress.

routes.name: Glen Ample and Beinn Each
routes.text: From Ardchullarie on Loch Lubnaig, the forest path to the head of Glen Ample, over Beinn Each and along a very rough, rocky ridge.
